content: European card-issuing authorities need a shared TACHOnet service to coordinate driver smart-card requests across participating member organizations. Users should be able to ask one or more members about the possible delivery or status of cards, receive standardized replies, and follow each request through completion. The service should also manage access rights, alert participants when expected replies are late, and provide operational statistics.

The main purpose is to let the card-issuing authorities coordinate driver smart-card matters across countries without everyone having to chase each other individually by email or phone. In practice, one authority can send a standardized request to one or several other participating authorities to check delivery status, validate whether a card exists, or follow up on a card-related issue, and then get a standard reply back.
The idea is that each authority remains responsible for its own cards and records, but they collaborate through a shared service so the exchange is consistent, traceable, and easier to monitor. They’re expected to respond within agreed timeframes, and the platform helps track requests until they are closed.

Yes, there are some practical limits, mainly driven by who is participating and what agreements are in place between them. My understanding is that an authority can only use the service with other member organizations that are onboarded and authorized for that exchange, and the exact request types allowed may depend on the process rules we agree for the network.
I don’t think it’s meant to vary much by card type in the system itself, but some request categories may be restricted if the receiving authority is not responsible for that card or if the data is not available for sharing. If there are country-specific legal or operational constraints, those would need to be enforced as part of the setup, but I’d need to confirm the exact rule set with the domain owners.

First, the organization has to be admitted as a participating member and have its access rights set up in the service. After that, its technical connection and operational parameters need to be configured so it can send and receive standardized requests and replies.
Once it has been tested and approved, it can start exchanging with the other authorized members. I’m not sure if there is a formal certification step in every case, but some kind of verification before go-live would definitely make sense.

A successful exchange is one where we get a standardized response that actually answers the request and can be matched back to the original case without ambiguity. Timeliness matters too, because if the reply comes too late it may no longer be operationally useful, even if it eventually arrives.
From our point of view, it also needs to be traceable end to end, so we can see when it was sent, who received it, what came back, and whether the case is closed or still pending. If the request is rejected or cannot be fulfilled, that can still count as a handled exchange as long as the reason is clear and recorded.

In practice, the exchanges have to follow the applicable European and national rules for driver card handling, plus the agreed TACHOnet procedures and any data protection obligations. That means authorities should only send the minimum information needed for the request, only use the data for the permitted administrative purpose, and keep it for as long as the rules allow.
The standards also shape how we respond, because replies need to be standardized and defensible, not informal. Retention and access are usually quite controlled, but I’d need to verify the exact legal retention periods and any country-specific restrictions with the compliance team.

The retention period is usually driven by the legal and administrative recordkeeping rules that apply to driver card operations, along with audit and traceability requirements for the service. In other words, we keep the records long enough to prove what was requested, who handled it, and how it was resolved, but not longer than the applicable rules require.
I would expect there to be some country-specific differences, especially where national public-records or privacy laws impose shorter or longer limits. I can’t give you the exact period without checking the specific legal framework for each participating authority.

Usually the compliance check happens after the exchange has been completed or at least after the response is received, rather than blocking every message in real time. They would review whether the request was sent by an authorized user, whether the right authority was contacted, whether only permitted data was shared, and whether the response followed the agreed standard.
They’re also checking that the case was closed properly and that there’s a traceable record for audit purposes. If something looks off, they’d flag it for correction or investigation before it’s treated as fully compliant.

It would need to happen earlier if the request itself is sensitive, incomplete, or outside the normal rule set, because then we may want to stop it before it goes out. That could be the case if the requester doesn’t have the right access, the target authority isn’t eligible for that exchange, or the request includes data that looks broader than necessary.
In those cases, the earlier review would check authorization, purpose, data minimization, and whether the request fits the approved workflow. I’d expect those to be exceptions rather than the normal path.

The main business scenario is one authority asking another whether a driver card can be delivered, confirmed, or otherwise traced, and then following that request until there’s a clear result. We also need to handle cases where several members are contacted in parallel, where a reply is late or never comes, and where the exchange ends in a refusal, a status update, or a completed delivery.
The operating boundaries are that only participating and authorized authorities can use the service, and they should only exchange the standardized card-request information needed for the administrative purpose. Everything has to stay traceable for operational follow-up and audit, but I’d expect the exact limits on statuses and exceptions to be defined in the agreed procedures.

Each step needs to be recorded with enough detail to reconstruct the exchange later: who initiated it, which authority it was sent to, when it was sent, what status it had, and what the reply or refusal was. If the status changes, that change should be timestamped and linked to the same request so we can see the full history rather than just the final state.
For audit, we’d also expect the record to show whether the response was on time, whether any reminders or alerts were issued, and whether the case was closed normally or escalated. The exact field set would come from the TACHOnet procedures and internal logging rules, but the principle is that nothing important should be left as an untraceable free-text note.

At submission, we’d need a unique request identifier, the sending authority, the receiving authority, the card or driver reference being queried, and the request type or purpose. We’d also want the submission timestamp and the current status so the case can be tracked from the start.
If there are any priority flags, due dates, or correlation details from a previous exchange, those should be captured too. I’m assuming the exact data items are whatever the standardized TACHOnet message set requires, but those are the basics we’d need operationally.

If a reply is overdue, the request should move into a clearly defined “pending overdue” or equivalent exception status rather than staying as simply open. That status should trigger whatever follow-up is agreed, usually a reminder or alert to the receiving authority and, if needed, escalation to the operator or compliance team.
If no reply arrives within the defined limit, the case should be closed only with a documented non-response outcome, not silently dropped. The exact thresholds and escalation steps should be consistent across members so everyone handles late responses the same way.

Each parallel inquiry should still tie back to one master request ID, and every recipient should get its own linked sub-reference or message instance under that master case. That way each reply, refusal, reminder, or non-response is recorded against the same originating inquiry, but you can still see which authority produced which outcome.
If one member answers and another doesn’t, both results stay visible in the same case history rather than being merged into a single summary. That linkage is what keeps the audit trail clear and avoids confusion later when someone reviews the file.

The first priority should be the core exchange flow: submit a request, route it to the right member authority or authorities, receive the standardized response, and track the case to closure with a complete audit trail. That gives the immediate business value because it lets authorities coordinate card requests and see the outcome reliably.
Things like richer analytics, advanced dashboards, more detailed SLA reporting, or extra automation around escalation can wait for a later phase. I’d also treat any nonessential convenience features, like broader search or more complex filtering, as secondary until the main tracking and notification behavior is stable.

An acknowledgment should count as accepted only if it comes from an authorized member and confirms receipt in the expected message format. If it only says the message was received but doesn’t address the actual request, I’d treat it as pending rather than fully answered.
If the acknowledgment is malformed, from an unauthorized source, or cannot be matched to the original request, it should not close anything and should probably be flagged for review. Any fallback behavior, like retrying or waiting for a proper response, should follow the agreed operational rules so we don’t accidentally treat a technical acknowledgement as a business answer.

A request should be marked overdue once the agreed response deadline has passed without a valid reply or accepted acknowledgment, and only then should escalation begin. Until that deadline is reached, it should remain in the normal awaiting response state.
At the escalation point, we’d need to record the deadline used, the timestamp when it became overdue, what reminder or escalation was triggered, and to whom it was sent. It would also help to log the current request state, the recipient authority, and any prior follow-up attempts so the audit trail shows exactly why the escalation happened.

I’d leave the exact list of escalation and reminder event types undecided for now. We know the audit trail must capture the fact that reminders, overdue notices, and escalations happened, but I think the precise event taxonomy can be agreed with the operations and compliance people later.
What matters at this stage is that every such event is timestamped, tied to the right request, and traceable back to the receiving authority. That gives us enough structure without locking ourselves into an overly detailed rule set too early.

Yes, those boundary cases should be handled explicitly, because they affect how readable the audit trail is. Repeated reminders should each be logged as separate events, multiple recipient authorities should each keep their own linked event history under the master request, and if an escalation follows a partial reply, that partial reply needs to stay visible so it’s clear why escalation still happened.
The key rule is that nothing should overwrite or hide earlier actions. Each event needs to link back to the original request and also to the specific recipient or response it relates to, so later reviewers can reconstruct the full sequence without ambiguity.

The timing and accuracy matter most when a request is blocking a driver card issue, especially if a citizen or authority is waiting on a status confirmation or delivery decision. In those cases, a delayed or unclear reply has real operational impact, so it needs to stay open and visible until we have a valid, unambiguous answer.
If a reply is late, we should keep the case in awaiting response and trigger the agreed reminder or escalation path. If it’s incomplete or ambiguous, it should not be treated as final; it should either stay pending or be flagged for clarification, with the original response preserved in the audit trail exactly as received.

That isn’t something I can give you as a fixed number right now. I’d expect the response time to be defined by the participating member agreements or the operational service levels, and it may vary depending on the type of request or whether it’s a normal case or an urgent follow-up.
For now, I’d say the system should work with configurable deadlines rather than a single hardcoded response time.

Yes, there will likely need to be differences, but I don’t want to lock them down too early. A standard status check may have a normal deadline, while a follow-up on an already overdue card issue could justify a shorter internal target or a different escalation path.
I’d also expect some exceptions for urgent or exceptional cases, but those rules should probably be configurable rather than hardwired. The important thing is that the system can support different deadlines by request category or priority without changing the core workflow.

Once it’s closed, it should move to a completed or closed state and stop generating normal workflow reminders. I would expect a final audit entry and probably a completion notification to the requesting party, so they know the case is finished.
If a new issue comes up later, that should usually be a new request rather than reopening the old one, unless there was a clear mistake or incomplete processing that the operations team decides should be corrected in the same case.

In practice, it should stay pending and be marked as needing clarification, because we don’t want to close it on an uncertain answer. If the workflow allows it, the system should send a clarification request back to the same authority and keep the original reply attached so nothing is lost.
The main exception would be if the ambiguity is minor and a human operator can resolve it locally without going back to the member, but that should be an explicit manual decision rather than automatic handling.

The practical rule should be whether the missing or unclear part can be resolved from information already in the request or from our own records without making assumptions. If the operator would have to guess, or if the answer affects the legal or operational meaning of the request, then it should go back for clarification.
If it’s just a formatting issue or a small wording ambiguity and the intent is still obvious, then a human operator can correct or interpret it locally, with that decision recorded in the audit trail.

We should record at least whether it is a request about delivery, a request about status, or a follow-up on a previously submitted card matter. In day-to-day use, that distinction matters because the handling and expectations can be different.
I don’t think the type should depend on the channel itself, but it may depend on the reason for the inquiry or the role of the authority making it. If that reason changes the workflow or the deadline, then it should be captured as part of the request metadata.

The practical rule should be that if the reason or role changes who is allowed to see the request, who should answer it, or how quickly it must be handled, then it has to be recorded as structured metadata and used by the workflow. If it is only descriptive and does not change processing, then it can be kept as reference information.
So in effect, anything that affects routing, access control, escalation, or deadlines should drive the processing path, while everything else should just be stored for traceability.

“Card availability status” should tell us the actual state of the card in terms of whether it can be delivered or is already in circulation. I’d expect something like available means it can be issued or dispatched, unavailable means it cannot be provided right now, pending means it is still being processed, and issued means it has already been delivered or completed.
The standardized response should always carry that status in a common format, plus any supporting dates or references that explain why that status was returned. If the status is unavailable or pending, the response should also make clear whether a later follow-up is expected or needed.

An expiry or reassessment date makes sense when the status is temporary, like pending, under review, or unavailable for a known period. In those cases, we want the system to know when to check again or when the answer might no longer be reliable.
Yes, some statuses can stay unchanged until a specific event occurs, like issued staying issued until there is a formal correction, or unavailable staying unavailable until the member reports a change. For those, I’d expect the event itself to trigger the next update rather than a fixed follow-up date.

It should stop treating the status as current when the event that was expected to change it has actually been detected or when the information becomes stale beyond an agreed validity period. If we have a known trigger, like a card being dispatched or a member sending a correction, that should automatically prompt reassessment.
If there is no specific event, then a validity timeout should apply so the system does not keep showing an old status forever.

I don’t know the exact endpoint name or URL yet, because that would depend on the technical API design we agree with the implementation team. From a requirements point of view, we should define a single standard service endpoint or service entry point for member systems, but the concrete path and protocol still need to be specified.
What matters is that all participating members use the same published interface for requests, replies, and status updates, rather than each one using a separate bespoke connection.

In principle, the shared endpoint should be available continuously, because member systems may need to send requests and receive replies at any time. Planned maintenance is the main exception, and that should be announced in advance with a clear outage window.
I wouldn’t want to build in business-hour restrictions unless there is a policy reason, because late replies and asynchronous updates are part of the service. Emergency access outside normal availability should also remain possible if the technical platform is up, even if some back-office follow-up happens later.

Yes, participation and request handling should be limited to onboarded members that are explicitly authorized for the relevant exchange. In practice, a request should only go to authorities that are part of the agreed network and permitted to handle that card or case type.
There can also be legal and responsibility boundaries, so the receiving authority should only be expected to answer within its own competence and national rules. If a request falls outside that scope, the system should record that limitation and route or reject it according to the agreed coordination rules.

In practice, I’d expect the default to be a standardized rejection or “cannot process” reply if the receiving authority has no competence at all. If there is another clearly responsible authority and the routing rules are known, then rerouting would be better, but that should only happen when the service can do it safely and with traceable responsibility.
Returning it for clarification makes sense when the request is incomplete or the authority cannot tell whether it is actually in scope. The choice between those paths should depend on whether the issue is missing information, wrong destination, or a genuine legal or operational exclusion.

First it should send it back as incomplete or unprocessable with a clear standardized reason, rather than guessing. That keeps the responsibility with the originating member to correct the request or resend it to the right place.
Only if the service has enough routing evidence should it try to forward it automatically. If not, it should avoid making assumptions.

The rule should be based on the best-known cause at the point the receiving authority evaluates the request. If the request is missing mandatory data, the code should say incomplete information; if it is outside the authority’s remit but obviously sent to the wrong place, it should say wrong destination; and if neither is clear, it should use a generic processing boundary code.
I’d want the wording to stay standardized across all members so the originating side can act on it consistently, but still be specific enough to tell them whether to correct the content or resend elsewhere.

Yes, if the more specific cause would require the receiving authority to reveal sensitive internal rules, legal interpretation, or operational details, then it should fall back to the generic boundary code. Also, if the evidence is weak or mixed and the authority cannot confidently classify it as incomplete data or wrong destination, the generic code is safer.
That way we avoid over-asserting a reason that might not be fully defensible while still giving the originating member a clear signal that the request cannot be processed as sent.

The retention rule should be the longest mandatory period that applies to that authority for the kind of record in question, unless a national rule explicitly requires earlier deletion. In other words, the system should allow each authority to configure its own retention period within the shared framework, because privacy and public-records obligations can differ by country.
For operational traceability and audit, I’d expect at least the request metadata and status history to be kept for the required period, but the exact limit is something we’d need to verify with the legal and records teams.

If there is an active legal hold, dispute, or audit requirement, the record should be kept until that hold is released, regardless of the normal retention end. If there is no hold, then the default should be deletion or anonymization depending on what the national rule allows for that record type.
Which of those two happens should be driven by the authority’s retention policy for that category of data, because some records may need to be removed entirely while others can only be stripped of personal data.

If it’s incomplete or ambiguous, I’d keep the item pending and mark it as needing attention rather than treating it as a valid completion. An unexpected format should usually be handled the same way unless the system can safely map it to a known standardized response.
Retrying makes sense only if the problem looks technical, like a transmission or parsing issue; if it’s a content problem, the request should stay open until a valid acknowledgment is received.

If it can’t be matched to a request or it’s malformed, it should be flagged for review first, because that usually means there is something to investigate rather than just waiting. If the message is clearly unusable, I’d also keep it out of the normal workflow so it doesn’t accidentally advance or close anything.
Whether it stays pending depends on whether the original request is still otherwise awaiting a legitimate reply; the unmatched acknowledgment itself should not be treated as a completion.

Yes, there can be limits, but they would be based on each authority’s legal competence and the scope of the card or case type. Some requests may only be allowed to go to the issuing authority, or only to authorities that have a defined role for that kind of driver card action.
So participation is not always universal for every case type; it depends on whether that authority is permitted to handle that category under national rules and the agreed network profile.

A delivery failure should notify the originating authority, and if the failure is on a reply path, also the responding authority should be informed so they know the message did not get through. It should be repeated only when the failure looks temporary, like a transport outage or timeout, and after a defined number of attempts it should escalate to an operator alert.
If the failure is clearly permanent, like an invalid address or unauthorized recipient, I would suppress repeated retries and log it as a non-recoverable delivery issue.

Yes, there can be authority-specific rules, mainly depending on whether the failure happened on an outgoing request or on a reply, and who is responsible for monitoring that channel. Usually the originating authority is always informed first, and the responding authority is added when the failure concerns their reply or when they need to resend.
If a particular national setup has a supervising or administering role, that role can also be copied in for persistent failures, repeated timeouts, or cases that need operational intervention. The notification scope would change based on the authority’s configured responsibility model and any escalation rules they have agreed for the network.

Yes, I would expect some exceptions like that. Retries may be allowed only for technical transport failures and only on channels where the sender controls delivery, while they should be suppressed for business rejections or messages that have already been definitively answered.
Also, some message types may be too time-sensitive to retry many times, so they would go straight to escalation sooner, and in some setups the responding authority may own the retry action rather than the originating authority.

I’d limit retry eligibility mainly to technical transport cases. Anything that looks like a business-level rejection, a validation error, an unauthorized request, or a malformed message should not be retried, because resending it won’t fix the underlying problem.
There may be a few special operational exceptions, but in principle those non-technical failures should go straight to review or escalation rather than automatic retry.

I don’t know the exact peak volume yet, and I’d need to check with the participating authorities and any operational data we have. From a requirements point of view, we should define a target peak capacity and a safe degradation threshold so the service keeps running even during spikes.
If you want, I can help frame that as a capacity requirement in terms of requests per minute, concurrent requests, or daily peak batch volumes.

Yes, there should be a defined recovery expectation, but I don’t know the exact target yet. In practice, participating authorities should see a clear service-unavailable status and keep their requests queued or deferred according to the agreed operating mode, rather than silently failing.
For restoration, I would expect an agreed recovery time objective and a fallback procedure, but the exact time and whether a secondary site is required would need confirmation from the operational owners.

In practice, I’d expect queued requests to remain stored until the service is restored, rather than being rerouted automatically, because rerouting could break the coordination and audit trail. The fallback mode should apply only when the central TACHOnet service or its core messaging path is confirmed unavailable, and participating authorities should be told to hold new traffic or follow a predefined manual contingency process.
If there is a separately approved alternate path, that would need to be explicitly configured and governed, but I would not assume automatic rerouting by default.

Yes, I would expect planned maintenance windows to be allowed, because this kind of service will need patching and operational work. They should be scheduled outside normal business peaks where possible, and participants should get advance notice, though I don’t know yet whether that means 24 hours, 48 hours, or something longer.
I’d also expect the outage window to be bounded and published in advance, with emergency maintenance treated separately and notified as soon as practicable.

For standard maintenance, I’d expect at least 48 hours’ notice, and for longer or more disruptive work, probably several business days’ notice. If it’s urgent security or incident-driven maintenance, that notice could be shorter, but it should still be communicated as soon as possible to all participants.
The exact split between maintenance types would need agreement, but I’d definitely keep emergency work as an exception rather than the norm.

We should treat it as confirmed once the planned maintenance starts at the published time, or earlier if the service owner sends an explicit notice that the outage has begun or is unavoidable. At that point participating authorities should switch to the hold-or-contingency process immediately rather than waiting for a failed request.
If the maintenance is only a warning or a possible delay, then I would not trigger the contingency yet.

Yes, a partial outage should trigger it earlier if it affects the message flow or response handling in a way that makes the service unreliable. For a phased shutdown, I’d apply the hold-or-contingency process when the affected function that participants depend on is actually taken out of service, not just when preparatory work starts.
If a maintenance notice is withdrawn, then the contingency should not start at all, or should be ended immediately if it had already been announced in error.

I don’t have a firm number agreed yet, but I’d expect the target to be relatively tight because participants depend on the service for operational coordination. A complete outage would need the fastest restoration target, while a partial interruption could have a slightly longer one if the core messaging and audit trail remain intact.
Planned maintenance is a bit different because it’s scheduled, so the main expectation there is to come back within the published maintenance window rather than a separate recovery target.

The rule should be based on the request state and the receipt of a valid acknowledgment, not just on whether the participant sees a network timeout. If a message was sent but no confirmation is received within the agreed timeout, the participant can retry once or follow the defined retry policy, but if the original request is later confirmed as accepted, duplicates should be suppressed.
If the exchange is explicitly rejected or still unresolved after the allowed retry window, then it should be treated as failed and escalated to operations for follow-up.

No, not for those cases. If the request is rejected for business reasons, fails validation, is unauthorized, or is malformed, it should go straight to review or escalation rather than being retried automatically.
A retry only makes sense for transport or transient technical problems, not for messages that are wrong or not permitted.

Yes, I’d expect status-check requests that are blocking an operational decision to have a tighter deadline than routine informational queries. Anything tied to an active card issuance case, a suspected duplicate, or an urgent status confirmation should escalate sooner if it is nearing the timeout because those directly affect next steps.
Routine background queries can wait for the standard response window, but urgent operational messages should move to escalation as soon as the delay starts to risk the business process.

I don’t have an agreed numeric peak yet. My expectation would be that it should handle the normal daily operating peak without noticeable delay, and then begin graceful degradation only beyond that point rather than failing outright.
Lower-priority work like statistics, reporting, or non-urgent follow-ups could be deferred first, while live request coordination should stay available as long as possible.

A member organization should not go fully live until its access rights are approved and its technical connection has passed the required interoperability and security checks. In practice, I’d also expect test exchanges to be completed successfully before they are allowed onto the live flow.
I can imagine a limited pilot or sandbox-style exchange starting earlier, but only if that is explicitly authorized and restricted to a controlled scope. If any checks are still pending, I would not let them participate in the production coordination flow.

Successful test approval should be treated as a mandatory gate for production exchanges, with no exceptions in the normal process. If something is still pending, that organization can stay in a controlled test or pilot mode, but not in live production coordination.
The only exception I’d expect is if there is a formally approved emergency arrangement from the program owners, and that would still need to be tightly limited and tracked.

Only under a formally approved temporary access arrangement, and even then it should be very limited and time-bound. I would expect that to be used only for exceptional operational need, with explicit authorization from the program owners and clear tracking of what they are allowed to do.
Otherwise, they should wait until the interoperability and security checks are fully complete before receiving live exchange access.
